questions.prompt: In Taleb's opening turtle story, what principle does Mercury enforce by refusing the meal?
choices: The people who created the bad outcome should bear it themselves
Bad decisions become fair once everyone shares the blame verbally
A risky offer is acceptable if the person receiving it can still refuse

explanation.gentle: Mercury's refusal matters because he will not let a burden be shifted onto someone who had no part in creating it. The story anchors the chapter's fairness rule before any technical examples arrive.
explanation.direct: The turtle story establishes downside ownership. The chooser does not get to export the pain after the choice turns bad. The other options soften the issue into language or procedure, which is not what the story does.
explanation.competitive: Mercury blocks the classic insulated move: keep the decision, dump the mess. The scene is not about politeness. It is about forcing consequence back onto the party that created it.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecture-agent anecdote matter to the chapter's argument?
choices: It shows that tax law is too complex for international speaking work
It shows how advice can sound helpful while leaving the advisor insulated from later downside
It proves that all agents eventually become hostile to their clients

explanation.gentle: The story matters because the agent's gain arrived at the moment of agreement, while Taleb met the later cost alone. That is the asymmetry the chapter wants you to notice.
explanation.direct: The anecdote exposes pseudo-advice. The agent used the language of benefit while staying outside the eventual tax problem. The point is structure, not universal hostility from agents or abstract tax complexity.
explanation.competitive: The commission was real. The care language was camouflage. Once the downside arrived, the agent's exposure vanished, which is exactly why the story belongs in this chapter.

questions.prompt: A coworker urges you to adopt a vendor he praises as perfect for your team, but he receives a referral fee and bears no cost if the rollout fails. Which chapter principle is most relevant?
choices: The problem is only legal if the fee is hidden in the contract
The recommendation is safe because referral fees are normal in business
The recommendation should be judged by who carries the downside, not by the confidence of the pitch

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps pushing you back to exposure. Referral fees may be common, but the real question is whether the recommender shares the cost if the recommendation hurts you.
explanation.direct: Shared downside is the diagnostic. The coworker may still be sincere, but the recommendation becomes weaker when his upside is immediate and your downside is unilateral.
explanation.competitive: Normal is not the same as clean. If he gets paid now and you eat the failure later, the structure is telling you more than his enthusiasm is.

questions.prompt: Lena is reviewing a software contract after a salesman spends twenty minutes telling her the switch will be great for her team. What is the strongest next move?
choices: Ask what he gains if she signs and what downside he shares if the promised savings fail
Focus on whether he sounds sincere enough to justify trust
Ignore the incentive question if the product demo looked polished

explanation.gentle: Lena needs to test exposure, not charm. Once she asks about his gain and his share of the downside, the recommendation becomes easier to evaluate clearly.
explanation.direct: The chapter says tone is weak evidence compared with shared risk. Asking about incentive and downside-sharing reveals whether the pitch is aligned or insulated.
explanation.competitive: Polish is cheap. Exposure is expensive. Lena wins the decision the moment she drags the salesman out of helper mode and into incentive mode.

questions.prompt: Which situation best fits Taleb's distinction between honest selling and disguised advice?
choices: A seller openly says he wants your business and explains the product from his side
A seller hides his incentive and frames the recommendation as if it were neutral guidance for your benefit
A buyer asks several questions before committing to a purchase

explanation.gentle: Taleb is much more suspicious of the second situation because hidden motive prevents the listener from judging the recommendation properly.
explanation.direct: Declared selling is cleaner because motive is visible. Disguised advice preserves informational advantage by pretending there is no angle to discount.
explanation.competitive: The ugliest move is not selling. It is selling while pretending not to be selling. That is where the asymmetry deepens.

questions.prompt: A classmate argues that every market involves uncertainty, so Taleb's complaint about asymmetry is unrealistic. What is the strongest reply from this chapter?
choices: Taleb wants markets to eliminate all uncertainty before any deal can be fair
Taleb distinguishes ordinary shared uncertainty from cases where one side is protected by knowledge the other side does not have
Taleb believes uncertainty matters only in finance, not in everyday exchange

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not asking for perfect information. It is asking whether one side knows enough to stay protected while the other side remains exposed.
explanation.direct: Ordinary uncertainty is compatible with trade. The violation begins when unequal information hardens into one-sided protection and exported downside.
explanation.competitive: Saying all markets are uncertain is a dodge. The real question is who knows where the blast radius is and who still has to stand in it.

questions.prompt: A student-club board recommends a meal-box partner without clearly disclosing that one member's sibling works there. Later the service fails. Which part of the failure matters most through this chapter's lens?
choices: The hidden relationship made the recommendation structurally dirtier than a plain bad judgment call
The only real issue is that the vendor underperformed operationally
The board member's family tie is irrelevant because no money changed hands directly

explanation.gentle: Bad performance hurts, but hidden motive changes how members would have interpreted the recommendation from the start. That is why trust falls so sharply.
explanation.direct: The undisclosed tie matters because it altered the epistemic position of everyone receiving the recommendation. Operational failure exposed the vendor weakness, but hidden incentive exposed the structural weakness.
explanation.competitive: Late meal boxes annoy people. Hidden angles make them feel used. The second problem is what detonates trust.

questions.prompt: Ruth's cousin says a startup investment is basically certain, but his own shares were granted through work rather than bought with fresh savings. What is Ruth's best test?
choices: Accept the pitch because family members usually know the founder better than outsiders do
Ask whether he would put new money in beside hers on the same terms and timeline
Ignore the recommendation completely because interested people are always lying

explanation.gentle: The smart move is to test shared exposure. If he would match the risk with fresh money, his recommendation carries more weight. If not, the confidence means less.
explanation.direct: This is a revealed-preference test. Matching the investment under the same conditions converts talk into shared downside. The other options either surrender to familiarity or collapse into blanket cynicism.
explanation.competitive: Ruth needs symmetry, not speeches. Fresh cash on the same terms tells the truth faster than family confidence ever will.

questions.prompt: What makes Rav Safra's story deeper than a simple rule about disclosing defects in merchandise?
choices: It shows that a fair deal depends partly on whether the seller stays honest about his own inward commitment, not only the product's condition
It proves that silence is always legally equivalent to accepting the highest later bid
It shows that bargaining itself should be abolished in favor of fixed pricing

explanation.gentle: Rav Safra matters because fairness reaches into intention here. He feels bound by the first price once he has accepted it inwardly, even though a higher price later appears.
explanation.direct: The story expands fairness beyond defect disclosure into self-discipline. He refuses to monetize another person's mistaken reading of his silence once he knows what the clean price is.
explanation.competitive: Rav Safra rejects the profitable loophole after it appears. That is what turns the story from compliance into character under temptation.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1 asks who eats the turtle in a single transaction. Which extension best prepares the logic for Chapter 2?
choices: Ask what happens when a small group can refuse change while a larger group keeps paying the adjustment cost
Assume the same fairness rule stops mattering once many people are involved
Treat system-level conflicts as too large to analyze through downside ownership

explanation.gentle: This chapter's logic scales by asking who keeps the burden of adjustment when many people are involved. That is the doorway into minority rule.
explanation.direct: The next conceptual move is from deal-level asymmetry to system-level asymmetry. If one side is harder to move, the other side may keep absorbing the cost of adaptation.
explanation.competitive: The turtle question does not disappear at scale. It gets bigger. Chapter 2 asks what happens when a stubborn minority can make the majority eat the adjustment.
